title: Problem Overview
content: **Erdős Problem #788** asks to estimate f(n), the maximum guaranteed |C|+|B| when B ⊂ (2n,4n) and C ⊂ (n,2n) is sum-free with respect to B. This is a min-max problem: the adversary picks B, we respond with C. Choi (1971) conjectured f(n) ≤ n^{1/2+o(1)}. The current best bounds are n^{1/2} ≪ f(n) ≪ (n log n)^{2/3}, with the gap open for over 50 years.
mathContext: The interval pairing is natural: elements c₁, c₂ ∈ (n, 2n) always sum to values in (2n, 4n). So B 'blocks' certain sums, and C must avoid producing those blocked sums. The function f(n) measures the tradeoff between blocking and avoiding.

title: Intervals and Sum-Free Property
content: **openInterval a b** = (a,b) ∩ ℕ via Finset.filter. **lowerInterval n** = (n, 2n), **upperInterval n** = (2n, 4n). **pairwiseSums C** collects all c₁ + c₂ for distinct c₁, c₂ ∈ C. **isSumFreeWithResp C B** requires c₁ + c₂ ∉ B for all distinct c₁, c₂ ∈ C. **sumFree_iff_disjoint** axiomatizes the equivalence with Disjoint(pairwiseSums C, B).
mathContext: The sum-free-with-respect-to condition generalizes classical sum-free sets: instead of avoiding all sums within S, we avoid sums landing in a specific target set B. This makes the problem a two-player game between B and C.

title: The Function f(n)
content: **isValidConfig n B C** requires B ⊆ upperInterval(n), C ⊆ lowerInterval(n), and C sum-free w.r.t. B. **f** is axiomatized as a function ℕ → ℕ giving the maximum k such that for all B, there exists a valid C with |C| + |B| ≥ k. Axiomatized since computing f(n) for general n requires deep combinatorial arguments.
mathContext: f(n) is the value of the min-max game: min over B of max over C of (|C| + |B|). The key question is the growth rate: does f(n) grow like n^{1/2} (Choi's conjecture) or closer to n^{2/3}?

title: Choi's Results (1971)
content: **choi_upper_bound** axiomatizes f(n) ≤ C·n^{3/4} for some constant C > 0. **choiConjecture** is defined (not axiomatized) as the statement that for any ε > 0, eventually f(n) ≤ n^{1/2+ε}. Choi's 3/4 bound was the first upper bound; his conjecture that the true exponent is 1/2 remains the central open question after 50+ years.
mathContext: The o(1) notation in n^{1/2+o(1)} means: for any ε > 0, f(n) ≤ n^{1/2+ε} for all sufficiently large n. This is strictly weaker than f(n) = O(n^{1/2}).

title: Adenwalla's Lower Bound via Sidon Sets
content: **adenwalla_lower_bound** axiomatizes f(n) ≥ c·n^{1/2}. The construction uses Sidon sets: **isSidonSet S** requires all pairwise sums a+b (a ≤ b) to be distinct. **sidon_sets_exist** axiomatizes that Sidon sets of size ~√n exist in intervals of length n. Taking C as a Sidon set in (n, 2n) ensures pairwiseSums(C) has |C|² entries, all distinct, so at most |C|² of (2n, 4n) is 'hit.' This forces |C| + |B| ≥ c√n.
mathContext: A Sidon set (B₂ set) of size k has exactly k(k-1)/2 distinct pairwise sums. In (n, 2n), Sidon sets of size ~√n exist by probabilistic or algebraic constructions (using Singer difference sets or Erdős-Turán).

title: Hunter's and BSS Upper Bounds
content: **hunter_bound** axiomatizes f(n) ≤ C·n^{2/3+ε} for any ε > 0, improving Choi's 3/4 exponent to 2/3. **bss_bound** (Baltz-Schoen-Srivastav 2000) gives the current best: f(n) ≤ C·(n log n)^{2/3}. The BSS proof uses probabilistic construction of strongly sum-free sets via large random Sidon sets. The log n factor is a technical overhead from the probabilistic argument.
mathContext: The BSS bound (n log n)^{2/3} improves Hunter's n^{2/3+ε} by making the o(1) correction explicit as (log n)^{2/3}. Whether the log factor can be removed (giving f(n) = O(n^{2/3})) is itself open.

title: Interval Arithmetic
content: **interval_sum_range** is proved constructively: for c₁, c₂ ∈ (n, 2n) with c₁ ≠ c₂, their sum is either in (2n, 4n), ≤ 2n, or ≥ 4n. The proof uses by_cases on membership in upperInterval, with simp and omega handling the arithmetic. **sums_in_upper_interval** axiomatizes the stronger statement that the sum always lands in (2n, 4n), which requires the strict inequalities n < c₁, c₂ < 2n.
mathContext: The interval constraint is what makes the problem natural: if n < c₁ < 2n and n < c₂ < 2n with c₁ ≠ c₂, then 2n < c₁ + c₂ < 4n. This means every pairwise sum from C lands in the same interval as B.

title: Summary Theorem
content: **erdos_788_summary** combines the two main bounds: (1) the lower bound f(n) ≫ n^{1/2} (Adenwalla), and (2) the upper bound f(n) ≪ (n log n)^{2/3} (BSS 2000). The proof is constructive: `exact ⟨adenwalla_lower_bound, bss_bound⟩`. This captures the complete state of knowledge: the exponent of f(n) lies between 1/2 and 2/3, with Choi's conjecture predicting 1/2.
mathContext: The conjunction captures the best known bounds without asserting which is tight. The gap between 1/2 and 2/3 is the central open question. Closing it in either direction would be a significant advance in additive combinatorics.
